extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in comedy, freedom of expression, and legal/communal disputes in India
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing how allegations of insulting religious sentiments in stand-up comedy are treated by complainants, police, and courts (e.g., what counts as evidence, grounds for arrest, and reasons for denying bail). Focus is on Indian incidents involving communal sensitivities and public order concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearsal overheard jokes as basis for complaint/arrest
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaints and FIRs can be filed on the basis of jokes overheard during rehearsals (the article states the complaint 'was made on the basis of jokes overheard during rehearsals').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Police in this case accepted a complainant's claim about rehearsal jokes as sufficient grounds for arrest, even though the performance had not yet begun; the article quotes the SP saying the complainant overheard jokes while rehearsing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of visual evidence does not preclude arrest
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities may proceed with arrests despite absence of video or other visual proof ('there was no visual evidence... lack of video evidence or otherwise, was not a concern').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Indore SP explicitly downplayed the absence of visual evidence; reliance on witness statements/complainant claims was treated as adequate to register FIR and arrest persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior videos to establish 'intent' to insult
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier content (e.g., past videos) may be cited by police/complainants to demonstrate a performer's intent to insult religious figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SP referred to an April 2020 video in which the comedian joked about a Hindi song as showing 'intent' to insult Hindu deities; the past video (even if later deleted) was treated as corroborative evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uproar/ruckus at venue as justification to stop performance and make arrests
rubrics_metrics.description: Disorder at the venue prior to or during an event is used as a justification to stop performances and to arrest participants ('There was ruckus at the venue even before Faruqui could perform').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Police framed the immediate disturbance as a public-order risk that warranted intervention and contributed to decisions to detain performers and refuse bail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective culpability when one act causes controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: If one performer’s act provokes controversy, other performers in the same event may be treated as culpable or prevented from continuing ('When you four are going to do something together and the first act itself kicks up a controversy, why should the other three be allowed to continue?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities applied a group-liability rationale: planned group performances were assumed to share intent or purpose, so non-performing or later acts were still actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complaints from vigilante or ideological groups treated as actionable
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims lodged by local activist or vigilante groups (here, a Hindutva group) can trigger FIRs and arrests; police may even praise such groups for being 'active and alert'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes the FIR was filed on the basis of a complaint from the Hind Rakshak Sangathan and quotes the SP praising the group’s vigilance, indicating such complaints are operationally sufficient to prompt police action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of bail on grounds of potential law-and-order disruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts/police can refuse bail for arrested performers on the explicit ground that releasing them would 'disrupt law and order'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece reports multiple bail pleas were rejected citing disruption of public order as the reason; this is used as a practical, recurring ground to keep suspects detained pending trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mocking deities as basis for 'hurting religious sentiments' charges
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes perceived as mocking Hindu gods or goddesses are treated as sufficient basis to file charges for hurting religious sentiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Police initially said the comedian 'had allegedly mocked Hindu gods and goddesses' and booked him on that basis; the article frames such perceived mockery as the core substantive allegation in these cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-complaint deletion of content does not necessarily negate allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Removal of videos or content after a complaint is filed does not automatically prevent authorities from treating that content as evidence or pursuing charges ('a complaint was filed against that video too and it has since been deleted').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article shows that deleted content was still referenced by police as part of their case to show intent and past behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived communal identity of performer shapes public reaction to arrests
rubrics_metrics.description: The religion or community identity of an accused performer influences public criticism and perception of arrests (SP's claim: 'the uproar around Faruqui’s arrest was only because he was a Muslim').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not a legal standard, the article highlights that communal identity is invoked by officials and commentators to explain differential public responses and may affect discourse around enforcement decisions.
